name: The Scott household — a name from the post office's letter lists

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE RETURN, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The office's list of letters uncalled-for is a RETURN — its statement of what was still unclaimed on ONE day — and the paper reprinted one return over as many consecutive issues as it took, so the bound is dated by the return of June 1835 and not by the issue it was read in (T-0425). The earliest issue this project reads the name in is 1835-07-01, 1 day later; that gap is an accident of which impression an extraction pass reached, and it is not evidence. Somebody was writing to this name at Chicago by 1835-06-30 and at no stated time before it; nothing says when they came. The date lines the printings set, and how they were weighed, stand beside this rule in tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py.

present_on_scene_date.note: A letter was still waiting for this name at the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 6, on or after the scene date, so the corpus puts somebody expecting them at Chicago at 1835-07-01.

later_occupation.note: NONE RECORDED FOR 1835 — AND A TRADE IS RECORDED FOR 1839. This is a POINTER at `directories.people[].occupation_later` on this same record, derived by `tools/qualify_later_trades.py` and holding nothing that block does not already say. It is not a claim about the scene date: the 1835 occupation above still reads `none_recorded`, its grade has not moved, and no premises has been sought on the strength of it, because a directory of 1839 is evidence about 1839. It is written because the field a reader consults was asserting an absence this file contradicts three lines further down, and "no trade anywhere" and "no trade in the scene window, one printed 1839" are not the same fact (T-0693).

persons.note: GRADED BY THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER — rule G2e, applied 2026-09-04. This identity is inferred because that rung fired on the civic and press rows recorded on this card, which the resident-research corpus does not read. This programme's letter-list rule of 2026-09-02 would call it a projected resident on the absence of a research row; it is superseded here, and a no-find in one corpus is not a finding about another (T-0822). KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Scott, John' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 6 — dated 1835-07-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 2 times in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “J. Scott,” (f1839_v0065, printed page 41, ward 1, voting for William B. Ogden); the city register of 1839 — “John Scott” as school inspector (f1839_r0038, printed page 38). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes_date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches_scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Scott' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins J. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Scott, James A. | Letter. | September 28, 1887,” (second_presb_0295, printed page 171), admitted 1887-09-28 by letter. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Scott' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins J. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

resident_research.summary: No reliable record in the reviewed repository newspaper/reference corpus, Chicago directories, digitized county/local histories, institutional records and targeted exact/variant-name web sweep could be tied to this postal person with sufficient date/place/occupation/kinship discriminators. This is a documented no-corroboration result, not evidence that the person did not exist.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE LETTER LISTS (T-0378, T-0379). THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER, NOT AN ARGUMENT: every other record here argues for a household, and this one argues for a PERSON. `data/residents/` cannot carry a person outside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing — one member, no dwelling, no division, no trade, no family, no arrival beyond the paper's bound. tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py derives the set and prints every refusal, `--gate` proves no record here gained a roof, a trade or a second member, and docs/LIBERTIES.md L214 carries the change of scale.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. scott_john, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e1304 (a single entry); scott_john, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 — f1843_e2197 (a single entry); scott_john, Norris's Chicago directory of 1844 — n1844_e1568 (a single entry).

occupation_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this trade against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Scott, John, carpenter, South Branch, west side'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: REFUSED, AND THE REFUSAL IS THE RECORD. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 prints an address against this name in 1843 and this pass will not carry it back to 1835. The 1835 record prints no trade for this person, so there is no 1835 business for a later door to position. Minting one out of a directory printed after the scene date is the one thing this pass may never do. A refusal is written here rather than dropped so that a later run can see the address was read and ruled on, not missed (docs/ADDRESS-BACK-PROJECTION.md, clause 1).

residence_back_projection.note: REFUSED, AND THE REFUSAL IS THE RECORD. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 prints where this person lived in 1843 and this pass will not carry it back to 1835. The entry gives a WARD, which is a division of the Chicago of 1843 and not a street. The town's 1835 wards are not these wards — the city was not incorporated until 1837 — so the figure does not carry back at all. A refusal is written here rather than dropped so that a later run can see the address was read and ruled on, not missed (docs/RESIDENCE-BACK-PROJECTION.md, clause R4).
